analysis.one_liner: Lets uninsured Americans aged 55 to 64 buy into Medicare, with a tax credit covering three-quarters of the premium.
analysis.headline: The bill to let 55- to 64-year-olds buy into Medicare drew 112 cosponsors, but it never got a committee vote or a floor vote before the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would open Medicare to Americans between 55 and 65 who don't have coverage from an employer or a government program — people who often lose insurance when they retire or are laid off before Medicare starts at 65. Enrollees would pay a premium set at Medicare's average cost per person, and a refundable tax credit would cover 75% of it, with the enrollee paying the rest. Employers who now promise retiree health coverage could instead move those retirees onto the new Medicare buy-in and pay 25% of the premium plus the extras Medicare doesn't cover. The bill was referred to three House committees in May 2005, then to subcommittees, and never advanced further.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured Americans between 55 and 64 — early retirees, laid-off workers, and others too young for Medicare but too old or too sick to find affordable private coverage — would gain access to Medicare's doctor and hospital coverage by paying a premium, with the tax credit picking up three-quarters of the cost.

how_it_helps.text: It creates a new Medicare option for people 55 to 64 who are not covered by a group plan or a federal health program, giving them the same benefits as any Medicare enrollee.
Enrollees get a refundable, advanceable tax credit covering 75% of the monthly premium, so they pay only 25% out of pocket.
Early retirees with COBRA continuation coverage could enroll while keeping that COBRA coverage, smoothing the gap between leaving a job and reaching 65.
Premiums would be set at the government's estimate of Medicare's average per-person cost, not at a profit-inflated private rate.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers fund the 75% premium credit. Enrollees pay the remaining 25% of a premium set at Medicare's full average per-person cost — several hundred dollars a month for the 55-64 population, regardless of income — and the Treasury also loses the tax revenue the refundable credit costs.

drawbacks.text: The premium is set at Medicare's average per-person cost for the whole 55-64 population, and the 75% credit is the same for everyone — so a low-income enrollee and a wealthy one pay the same 25% share, which could still be several hundred dollars a month.

Employers offering retiree coverage may modify it to cover only what Medicare doesn't plus 25% of the premium, which could shift the cost of covering early retirees from employers to the federal credit.

Adding a new entitled population to Medicare increases federal outlays for their care, offset only by premiums and the enrollees' 25% share; the bill provides only trustee and GAO reports, not an automatic fix, if financing falls short.
Because eligibility excludes people who can get a group plan, the pool would skew toward people with high medical needs, which tends to push the average premium higher than the bill's estimate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people stranded without coverage in the years before Medicare, a guaranteed public plan at 25% of an average-cost premium is a substantial benefit, and the credit's flat design plus the employer cost-shifting option are real design weaknesses rather than fatal ones. The cost to the Treasury would be significant, but the bill would replace some of the most expensive kind of uninsured care with insured care.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to three House committees in May 2005, then sent to their health subcommittees, and it sat there — no markup, no vote, nothing more — until the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stark introduced the Medicare Early Access Act of 2005 in the House on May 4, 2005.
The bill was referred to the Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Education and the Workforce Committees, and within three weeks was sent to health and employer-employee relations subcommittees.

112 representatives signed on as cosponsors — 111 Democrats and 1 Independent — including the House Minority Leader, the ranking members of the two committees with jurisdiction, and other senior members.
No further action was ever recorded: the bill never received a subcommittee or committee vote and never reached the House floor before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.
Under House practice, referred bills die unless the committee chair schedules them for consideration; no such action was taken here.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private insurers kept the market for covering 55- to 64-year-olds without a competing Medicare option, and employers with retiree plans kept their existing arrangements. Near-retirees without coverage gained nothing — the coverage gap this bill targeted remained in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers and employers; near-retirees stayed uncovered

sides.party_line_note: All 112 cosponsors were Democrats plus one Independent, with no Republican support; the Republican-controlled committees never acted on the bill.

industries.note: Uninsured 55- to 64-year-olds are a market for individually purchased and short-term private coverage, and a Medicare buy-in would move many of them into a government plan instead. The bill's death left that private market intact.

The bill would let employers shift early retirees onto the Medicare buy-in while paying only 25% of the premium plus services Medicare doesn't cover, trimming a costly retiree benefit. Retirees would still be covered, so employers' savings run alongside the coverage benefit to workers.
More insured 55- to 64-year-olds would mean fewer unpaid bills for care delivered to people without coverage.
